intro:
AI phone answering for vegan restaurants helps you keep takeout orders moving when the phone is busy. It can answer the call, take the order from your live menu, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen.

For a vegan spot, that matters because callers often ask detailed menu questions. They may want to know what is dairy-free, what can be modified, or whether a dish is sold out. A phone host like ROAL can handle the simple stuff, then hand tricky questions to your team with a short summary.

sections.h2: What should an AI phone host do for vegan takeout?
sections.body:
For a vegan restaurant, the phone host should do the boring but important work fast and clearly. That means pickup orders, delivery orders from your live menu, hours, address, parking, and menu questions. It should also speak the caller’s language, collect the name and phone number, quote a ready time, and confirm the order back before sending it to the kitchen.

Here is a practical phone flow for a vegan takeout spot:

1. Answer with your restaurant name and takeout greeting.
2. Ask whether the caller wants pickup or delivery.
3. Take items, sizes, modifiers, and special notes.
4. Confirm the name, phone, and ready time.
5. Send the ticket to the kitchen screen.

Use a line like: “Thanks for calling Green Table. Would you like pickup or delivery today?”

For vegan menus, the host should also avoid offering sold-out items and should hand off allergy-sensitive questions to staff. If someone asks, “Does this contain honey?” or “Can you check the sauce ingredients?” the best move is to pass it along with a summary instead of guessing. ROAL is built for that kind of call handling, and it can be set up from your website or menu page in about a minute.

sections.h2: How do you forward calls without losing your main number?
sections.body:
Most owners want to keep their existing number. That is how ROAL works. The restaurant keeps its own number, and ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically after the host is claimed. You then forward your existing number to that line, either all calls or only when busy or unanswered.

For many phone systems, forwarding is easy, but the code depends on the carrier or system. On many landlines and some carriers, *72 followed by the forwarding number turns on forwarding, and *73 turns it off. On GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# often forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off. **61*number# often forwards unanswered calls, and **67*number# often forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless often uses *72 and *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually use a web portal. Codes vary, so confirm with your carrier and test with a real call.

Use this quick plan:

1. Decide whether to forward all calls or only missed/busy calls.
2. Confirm the correct code with your carrier or phone system.
3. Test one real call from a mobile phone.
4. Listen for the greeting and check the kitchen ticket.

If you need a handy reference, [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) can help you check the common options before you test.

sections.h2: What does a vegan caller need the host to get right?
sections.body:
Vegan callers often care about details. They may ask whether a sauce contains dairy, whether a dish has egg, or whether a side can be swapped. The host should not guess. It should answer what is on the menu, say when it is unsure, and move the rest to staff.

Here is a useful checklist for vegan takeout calls:

- Does the menu item use dairy, egg, honey, or other animal products?
- Can the kitchen mark a modifier, like no cheese or sauce on the side?
- Is the item sold out right now?
- What is the ready time for pickup?
- Does the caller need parking or entrance directions?

Example call line: “I can take your order and note that you want the tofu bowl with no mayo. For ingredient details I’m sending a note to the team.”

That approach keeps the call moving without making promises the kitchen cannot keep. It also helps with sensitive questions. If someone asks about allergies or says they need a manager, the host should hand it off with a summary. The same goes for complaints and catering questions. For menu-focused call handling, [menu, hours and allergen questions](/use-cases/menu-questions) is a good place to compare the workflow.

sections.h2: How do you use the dashboard to keep vegan orders organized?
sections.body:
A busy vegan restaurant needs a clear view of what is coming in and what is ready. ROAL’s dashboard gives you live tickets with statuses like new, preparing, and ready. If a caller later says, “I ordered the wrong side,” the transcript and recording help staff check what was said. If you run more than one location, you can keep menus separate by location.

sections.h2: When does a vegan restaurant still need a person on the phone?
sections.body:
Even with an AI phone host, some calls belong to staff. That includes allergy-sensitive questions, catering requests, complaints, and manager requests. It also includes anything the host could not answer from the menu or public pages. The goal is not to replace your team. It is to keep routine orders moving while people handle the calls that need judgment.

A simple handoff rule works well:

1. If it is a standard pickup order, let the host finish it.
2. If it is a menu detail the host knows, let it answer.
3. If it involves allergies, a complaint, or a manager, send it to staff.
4. If a caller asks for something sold out, suggest what is available instead.

Example handoff line: “I’m sending your question to the team with a summary so they can check the ingredients for you.”

That is especially helpful in vegan restaurants, where callers may care deeply about what is in the food. If the host cannot answer the first time, you answer once in the inbox and it learns from there. If you are ready to test a live call flow, you can [build a free test host](/try) from your website and hear how it sounds before you forward any calls.
